query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Enhanced free energy sampling that integrates metadynamics (or umbrella sampling) with thermodynamic integration across compositional and thermal degrees of freedom yields accurate and efficient predictions of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume changes at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties in high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Atomistic models of high-entropy alloys in their equilibrium solid and nascent liquid states near the melting point, spanning a broad range of near-equiatomic compositions.
generation.intervention: Perform high-fidelity atomistic simulations using enhanced sampling techniques (metadynamics/umbrella sampling) integrated with thermodynamic integration to traverse the free energy landscape around the melting transition.
generation.conditions: Simulations conducted at temperatures approaching melting across diverse HEA compositions under periodic boundary conditions, ensuring adequate sampling of both compositional and thermal fluctuations.
generation.structural_mediator: Detailed atomistic configurations that capture free energy barriers and transition states between the solid and liquid phases, thereby mediating the observed phase change phenomena.
generation.mechanism: By overcoming free energy barriers through enhanced sampling, the method accurately integrates over the free energy landscape, capturing subtle energetic and volumetric fluctuations during melting that govern thermodynamic properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The approach is expected to provide melting temperatures, fusion enthalpies and entropies, as well as volume change and liquid-phase properties with significantly reduced error margins compared to conventional isolated measurements or simplified models; anticipated improvements are on the order of tens-of-percent in both accuracy and efficiency, although precise values remain uncertain.
generation.baseline: Conventional simulation or experimental techniques that rely on isolated measurements or limited free energy estimates for each property.
generation.boundary: The approach is applicable to HEAs with near-equiatomic or moderately varying compositions at near-melting conditions; its performance may diminish if the alloy exhibits extreme compositional ordering or kinetic barriers that challenge sampling convergence.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative gains in accuracy and efficiency are not yet defined and depend on convergence of the sampling and the accuracy of the interatomic potentials used. Further experimental benchmarks are needed for validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Apply the integrated enhanced sampling method to compute melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, volume change at melting, and selected liquid-phase properties for a well-characterized set of high-entropy alloys. Compare the simulation outputs with high-precision experimental measurements obtained via calorimetry, in situ microscopy, and diffraction techniques.
measurements: Melting temperature (via calorimetry and in situ STEM heating)
Enthalpy and entropy of fusion (via differential scanning calorimetry)
Volume change at melting (via high-temperature X-ray diffraction)
Liquid-phase properties (via viscosity and density measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimentally measured thermodynamic properties differ from simulation predictions by margins exceeding predetermined uncertainty thresholds or if the efficiency and accuracy improvements over conventional methods are not statistically significant, then the proposed enhanced sampling approach must be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High entropy alloy nanoparticles bring hope to developing more efficient nanomaterials for high‐temperature applications. Nevertheless, the enhanced thermal stability of nearly equiatomic nanoalloys containing at least 5 metals is nothing more than theoretical speculation about the impact of thermodynamic contributions on their structural properties and remains to be proven. Here, in situ aberration‐corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and molecular dynamics simulations are combined to investigate at the atomic scale the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles (NPs) from 298 to 973 K. Both in situ STEM heating and atomistic simulations reveal strong structural and chemical evolutions in the NPs with the formation and melting of an AuCu layer at the surface of NPs at high temperature. This phase separation that appears progressively with temperature is driven by pronounced atomic diffusion that is surprisingly more active in these quinary nanoalloys than in monometallic and bimetallic subsystems.
